title: NY State Assembly · District 63
area: Staten Island's West Shore and North Shore, including Port Richmond, Mariners Harbor, Bulls Head, Travis and Westerleigh.

context.text: Both parties' primaries were canceled. Incumbent Samuel Pirozzolo advanced from the Republican and Conservative Party primaries unopposed; Matthew Mobilia advanced from the Democratic primary unopposed. This is a rematch of the 2024 general election, which Pirozzolo won 57.3%-42.2%.

summary.text: Samuel Pirozzolo is the Republican and Conservative incumbent Assembly Member for District 63, first elected in 2022 after losing a 2012 run for the same seat. A Staten Island native, he has operated his family's optical practice for more than three decades and previously served as president of Community Education Council 31. He is running for re-election; his campaign website lists bail law reform, support for the NYPD, property taxes and small-business support among his issues.

background.text: Pirozzolo is a native Staten Islander. According to his Assembly biography, he has operated his family's optical practice for 33 years; his campaign website describes more than three decades as a small-business owner.

He served as president of Community Education Council 31 for seven years and as Vice President of the New York City Parents Union. His Assembly biography cites a Gifted and Talented program for middle-school students and the cleanup of PCBs leaking from classroom light fixtures among his education-advocacy accomplishments.
In 2012 he was the Republican nominee for Assembly District 63 and lost the general election to incumbent Democrat Michael J. Cusick.

In 2022 he won the Republican primary over Paul Ciurcina Jr. on June 28 and was elected to the Assembly on November 8, 2022, defeating Democrat Vincent Argenziano for the open seat previously held by Cusick; he represents Staten Island's West Shore.
He was re-elected on November 5, 2024, defeating Democrat Matthew Mobilia, and appeared on the Republican and Conservative lines.
Assigned in 2025-2026 to the Children and Families, Economic Development/Job Creation/Commerce and Industry, Education, Energy, and Higher Education committees.

According to his campaign website, his work in office has included nearly $500,000 in grants to schools and community organizations, a $12 million portion of the state's Opioid Settlement Fund for Staten Island, and an expansion of the resident bridge-toll discount.

priorities.text: Opposes the siting and construction of battery energy storage systems in the district, citing fire and safety risks.
Opposes congestion pricing, green-energy mandates and other policies he says raise energy bills, tolls and taxes for working families.
Wants the city's property-tax assessment system updated, saying Staten Island's single- and two-family homes are taxed at higher effective rates than larger multifamily buildings.
Supports repealing cashless bail reform and backs the NYPD.
Says he has delivered funding for Staten Island schools, nonprofits and substance-abuse treatment providers.

positions.summary: His campaign issues page says he opposes congestion pricing, which it lists among policies that drive up costs for working families.
positions.quote: He opposes congestion pricing schemes, green energy mandates that spike your utility bill, and tax hikes disguised as investments.

positions.summary: Opposes green energy mandates that he says raise utility bills, according to his campaign's issues page.
positions.quote: green energy mandates that spike your utility bill

record.text: Prime-sponsored A00139, which would prohibit siting or construction of battery energy storage systems in Assembly District 63; held for consideration in the Local Governments Committee 13-5 on May 20, 2025.

Prime-sponsored A09019, which would prohibit the New York City mayor from residing in a rent-stabilized apartment and authorize a landlord to bring an eviction proceeding against the mayor; held for consideration in the Housing Committee 17-8 on May 20, 2026.
Prime-sponsored A00263, a constitutional amendment to lengthen Assembly and Senate terms to six years and impose term limits on legislators; referred to the Governmental Operations Committee.

Prime-sponsored A08927, which would prohibit cannabis retail licensees from operating a storefront within 500 feet of child day-care centers, public parks or playgrounds; referred to the Economic Development Committee.

candidates.name: Matthew Mobilia
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the Democratic primary unopposed after it was canceled; ran unsuccessfully against Pirozzolo in 2024.

summary.text: Matthew Mobilia is a Staten Island trial attorney and former Richmond County prosecutor running as the Democratic nominee against incumbent Samuel Pirozzolo for the second consecutive election. After law school he worked as a prosecutor and then a court attorney in Kings County Civil Court before opening his own law practice in 2022. His campaign website describes a platform built on public safety, the local economy, neighborhoods and human rights.

background.text: Born and raised in Staten Island; earned a B.A. in politics from Saint Anselm College and a J.D. from Albany Law School (2015).

After law school he worked as a New York City prosecutor in the Richmond County District Attorney's Office under DA Michael E. McMahon, handling cases including homicides, burglaries, DWI and narcotics offenses and trying cases to verdict; he spent four years there.
He then served as an Associate Court Attorney to Judge Matthew P. Blum of Kings County Civil Court, handling no-fault, commercial landlord-tenant, civil and small-claims matters.
Opened The Law Office of Matthew Mobilia in 2022, a practice handling criminal defense, personal injury and real estate matters.
He ran for Assembly District 63 in 2024 as a Democrat and lost the general election to incumbent Samuel Pirozzolo.

He is the 2026 Democratic nominee, also on the Affordable & Safe Party line. Describing himself as a seasoned trial lawyer and local business owner, his campaign website lists public safety, the local economy, neighborhoods and human rights as his four focus areas.

priorities.text: Public safety: stronger community policing, better law-enforcement training, and collaborative initiatives with community leaders.
Local economy: financial support and reduced regulation for small businesses to revitalize the local economy.
Neighborhoods: investing in local infrastructure, public services and educational initiatives.
Human and civil rights: opposing discrimination and injustice and promoting equal treatment.

candidates.researchNotes: Mobilia has not completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey and has never held elected office, so there is no official record. His campaign site states four broad priority areas but does not take specific positions matching this guide's fixed issue list; none are included rather than inferred from party or general statements.

Pirozzolo's and Tannousis's Assembly floor votes are overwhelmingly near-unanimous procedural bills; the two contested votes cited here were the only 2025-2026 floor votes in the repo's roll-call snapshot on which both Staten Island Republicans voted no.
